items.value: Statements I and III only: an Ordinance can amend a Central Act and can be given retrospective effect, but it cannot abridge a Fundamental Right
items.reasoning: Article 123(2) gives an Ordinance the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, so it can amend or repeal any Central Act (I correct) and, like an Act, can be made to operate from a back date (III correct). But Article 123(3) declares an Ordinance void so far as it makes any provision Parliament could not itself enact, and Article 13(2) bars Parliament from making any law that abridges a Fundamental Right; hence II is wrong. Options A, B and D all include II and therefore fail.

items.value: Only two pairs are correct — Arunachal Pradesh and Tripura; the Nagaland pair is wrong because Nagaland was created by an ordinary Act of Parliament, not a Constitutional Amendment Act
items.reasoning: I is correct: Itanagar takes its name from the Ita Fort ('ita' = brick), and Arunachal Pradesh has exactly two national parks, Namdapha and Mouling. III is correct: Tripura was a Part 'C' State, became a Union Territory under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (with the 7th Amendment abolishing Part C States) and became a full State in 1972. II is wrong: Nagaland came into existence under the State of Nagaland Act, 1962 — an ordinary law under Article 3, which Article 4 expressly says is not a constitutional amendment; the 13th Amendment only inserted Article 371A conferring special provisions. The State that actually came into existence through a Constitutional Amendment Act is Sikkim (36th Amendment, 1975). This is the contentious statement of the item — some prep material loosely credits the 13th Amendment with 'creating' Nagaland — hence MED.

items.value: Only one — the Inter-State Council; the National Security Council and the Zonal Councils are not constitutional bodies
items.reasoning: The Inter-State Council was set up in 1990 by a Presidential order issued under Article 263, so it is constitutional. The National Security Council was created in 1998 by an executive resolution of the government — neither constitutional nor statutory. The Zonal Councils are statutory bodies created by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (the North-Eastern Council by a separate Act of 1971), not by the Constitution. Hence only one.

items.value: Statement I only: the Constitution does expressly provide for the Governor acting in his discretion, but the President cannot reserve a State bill on his own
items.reasoning: Article 163(1) itself carves out functions the Governor is 'by or under this Constitution required to exercise in his discretion', and specific discretionary spheres are spelt out in Article 371A(1)(b) for Nagaland, Article 239(2) where a Governor administers an adjoining Union Territory, and paragraph 9(2) of the Sixth Schedule — so I is correct. Under Article 200 it is the Governor alone who may reserve a State bill for the President's consideration; the President has no power to call up a State bill suo motu, so II is wrong.

items.value: All three pairs are correctly matched — Article 50 (DPSP), Article 51A(f) (Fundamental Duty) and Article 24 (Fundamental Right)
items.reasoning: Article 50, a Directive Principle, requires the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State, matching I. Article 51A(f), a Fundamental Duty, requires every citizen to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture, matching II. Article 24, in Part III, prohibits employment of any child below fourteen years in a factory, mine or other hazardous employment, matching III. All three pairs stand.

items.value: Neither statement is correct — the State keeps its executive power in a Scheduled Area, and the Union can only give directions, never take over the whole administration
items.reasoning: Declaration of a Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule does not displace the State: the State's executive power continues, the Governor gains special powers to make regulations and to direct that a law shall not apply, and no local body takes over the administration — so I is wrong. Paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule requires the Governor to report annually to the President and extends the Union's executive power only 'to the giving of directions to the State as to the administration of the said areas'; giving directions is far short of taking over total administration, and no provision allows the Union to assume it on the Governor's recommendation — so II is wrong too. Both statements are of the absolute-overstatement type the Fifth Schedule deliberately avoids.

items.value: None of the pairs is correctly matched — the three ministries are cyclically shifted relative to the correct ones
items.reasoning: The National Automotive Board was set up under the Department of Heavy Industry and belongs to the Ministry of Heavy Industries, not Commerce and Industry. The Coir Board is a statutory body under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, not Heavy Industries. The National Centre for Trade Information is a joint venture of the India Trade Promotion Organisation and NIC and therefore sits under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not MSME. Every ministry listed is in fact the right ministry for a different organisation in the list, so nothing matches. The confidence is MED only because the whole answer turns on the placement of the relatively obscure National Automotive Board; the Coir Board and NCTI placements are certain.

items.value: I and II only — amending the Union List and Article 162 (extent of a State's executive power) needs State ratification; Article 158 on the conditions of the Governor's office does not
items.reasoning: The proviso to Article 368(2) lists the entrenched matters, which include 'any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule' — covering List I, so I qualifies — and expressly name Article 162, which is headed 'Extent of executive power of State', so II qualifies. The conditions of the Governor's office are governed by Article 158, which appears nowhere in that proviso; nor is Chapter II of Part VI among the entrenched chapters. Hence III does not require ratification by half the States, ruling out B, C and D.

items.value: All three are correct — Article 361(1), Article 361(2) and Article 194(2)
items.reasoning: Article 361(1) provides that the President and the Governor shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of their office, which is statement I verbatim. Article 361(2) bars the institution or continuation of any criminal proceedings whatsoever against the President or a Governor in any court during the term of office, which is statement II. Article 194(2) gives members of a State Legislature immunity from proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given in the House or its committees, which is statement III.

items.value: Only two — refining, storage and distribution of petroleum, and marketing and sale of petroleum products; production of crude oil and of natural gas are outside the Board's remit
items.reasoning: The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, 2006 defines a 'specified activity' as refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, marketing and sale of petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas, but expressly excludes the production of crude oil and natural gas. Upstream production is regulated instead by the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. So activities II and III fall to PNGRB while I and IV do not — two in all.

items.value: All three are correct — revenue deficit Rs 20,000 crore, fiscal deficit Rs 10,000 crore, primary deficit Rs 4,000 crore
items.reasoning: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts = 80,000 - 60,000 = Rs 20,000 crore, so I holds. The fiscal deficit is by definition the amount the government must borrow, i.e. total expenditure less total receipts other than borrowings; the budget shows borrowings of Rs 10,000 crore, so the fiscal deficit is Rs 10,000 crore and II holds. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments = 10,000 - 6,000 = Rs 4,000 crore, so III holds.

items.value: The INSTC links India through Iran to Central Asia, Russia and on to Europe
items.reasoning: The INSTC, agreed at St Petersburg in 2000 by India, Iran and Russia, is a roughly 7,200 km ship-rail-road network running from Indian ports to Bandar Abbas and Bandar-e-Anzali in Iran, across the Caspian to Russia and Central Asia, and onward to northern Europe, with a western branch through Azerbaijan. Option A names both the essential Iranian leg and the Central Asian and European legs. B is wrong because the corridor deliberately bypasses China and C describes the Kaladan/trilateral highway projects instead. D is the near miss: Azerbaijan is on one branch, but omitting Iran leaves out the leg that defines the corridor, so A is the better description.

items.value: Statement I is wrong (the United States, not Brazil, is the larger ethanol producer) while Statement II is correct (corn in the USA, sugarcane in Brazil)
items.reasoning: The United States has been the world's largest ethanol producer for well over a decade, producing roughly 15 billion gallons a year against Brazil's roughly 8 billion, so the claim that Brazil out-produces the USA is false. Statement II is factually right: American ethanol is overwhelmingly corn-based while Brazilian ethanol is overwhelmingly sugarcane-based. With I false and II true, only option D fits; A and B require both to be true and C requires I to be true.

items.value: Statement II only — at a wet-bulb temperature of 35 degrees Celsius evaporative cooling by sweating fails, threatening the survival of humans and other animals
items.reasoning: The wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature attainable by evaporating water into the air; once it reaches about 35 degrees Celsius, sweat can no longer evaporate fast enough to shed metabolic heat and even a healthy person resting in the shade cannot survive prolonged exposure. That is precisely statement II. Statement I lists flooding, cyclones and droughts, which are general consequences of a warming climate but are not what a wet-bulb threshold implies; the question asks specifically for the implication of the wet-bulb finding, so I does not follow.

items.value: Rs 48,500 crores — gross fiscal deficit minus interest payments
items.reasoning: Gross primary deficit = gross fiscal deficit - interest payments = 50,000 - 1,500 = Rs 48,500 crore. The non-debt creating capital receipts of Rs 10,000 crore are a distractor: they are already netted off in arriving at the fiscal deficit, so subtracting or adding them again would double-count. Option B adds the interest liability instead of subtracting it and C additionally folds the capital receipts back in.

items.value: Statements I, III and IV — the Rs 4,800 crore education grant, the Rs 45,000 crore agricultural-reform incentive and the reintroduction of tax effort as a criterion; the devolution share is 41 per cent, not 45 per cent
items.reasoning: Statement II is the decisive one and it is false: the 15th Finance Commission recommended that 41 per cent of the net proceeds of Union taxes be devolved to the States, one percentage point below the 14th Commission's 42 per cent to account for the reorganisation of Jammu and Kashmir into Union Territories. Since II is wrong, options A, B and D all fall away. The remaining three are right: the Commission recommended Rs 4,800 crore over 2022-23 to 2025-26 to incentivise better educational outcomes, Rs 45,000 crore as a performance-based incentive for agricultural reform, and it restored 'tax and fiscal efforts' (weight 2.5 per cent) as a devolution criterion after the 14th Commission had dropped it.

items.value: Statements I and III only — the IBRD lends to middle-income countries and was created to rebuild post-war Europe, but it does not work single-handedly
items.reasoning: The IBRD lends and provides guarantees to middle-income and creditworthy lower-income governments, which is statement I. It was established at Bretton Woods in 1944 with reconstruction of war-damaged Europe as its first mandate — its very name begins with 'Reconstruction' — which is statement III. Statement II is wrong on the word 'single-handedly': the IBRD is one of five World Bank Group institutions and works alongside the IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID, with the IDA in particular serving the poorest countries.

items.value: Statement I only — RTGS settles in real time and NEFT in batches, but inward RTGS transactions are free and both systems now run round the clock
items.reasoning: RTGS settles each instruction individually and continuously in real time, whereas NEFT settles in half-hourly batches, so I is correct. II is wrong because the RBI's own framework mandates that inward transactions in RTGS carry no charge to the customer; charges apply only to outward transactions. III is wrong because RTGS has been available 24x7x365 since December 2020 and NEFT since December 2019, so neither has restricted operating hours on certain days. Only statement I survives.

items.value: Only three — the United Arab Emirates, France and Singapore; Germany and Bangladesh do not accept UPI merchant payments
items.reasoning: NPCI International has enabled UPI acceptance at merchants in the UAE through the NEOPAY terminal network, in France through the Lyra tie-up that made it the first European country to take UPI, and in Singapore through the arrangement with NETS merchant terminals alongside the UPI-PayNow remittance linkage. Germany and Bangladesh have no such merchant acceptance arrangement. That gives three of the five. Confidence is MED because Singapore's case is sometimes described only in terms of the PayNow person-to-person link rather than merchant acceptance.

items.value: All three are correct — one crore rooftop installations, MNRE grassroots training on installation and maintenance, and over three lakh skilled personnel under capacity building
items.reasoning: PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, launched in February 2024, targets rooftop solar on one crore residential households, so I is correct. The scheme's capacity-building component is run by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy and includes training at the grassroots on installation, operation, maintenance and repair of rooftop systems, so II is correct. The same component sets out creating more than three lakh skilled personnel through fresh skilling and up-skilling, so III is correct. Confidence is MED because the exact three-lakh figure is a scheme-document detail rather than a widely reproduced headline number.

items.value: At the launch of the Quit India Movement
items.reasoning: Gandhi used the phrase in the course of the Quit India address to the AICC at Gowalia Tank on 8 August 1942, in the passage where he explains that although he preaches no hatred of the British he is himself openly disloyal to their government. Champaran in 1917 concerned a Section 144 order rather than sedition; his celebrated line at Dandi in 1930 was about shaking the foundations of the British Empire; and a declaration of sedition as one's religion would have been out of place in his address to the Second Round Table Conference in London. Confidence is MED because the sentiment is closest to his 1922 sedition-trial statement, which is not among the options.

items.value: Bronze
items.reasoning: The 'Dancing Girl' from Mohenjo-daro is a roughly 10.5 cm figurine cast in bronze by the lost-wax (cire perdue) process, and it is the standard textbook illustration of Harappan metal casting. Carnelian at Harappan sites appears as beads, terracotta (clay) is the material of the mother-goddess figurines and toys, and no gold figurine of this kind has been reported.

items.value: Madan Mohan Malaviya, with Krishna Kant, defended the Chauri Chaura accused
items.reasoning: After the Chauri Chaura incident of 4 February 1922 the Sessions Court sentenced 172 of the accused to death. Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya, himself a lawyer, took up their defence in the appeal before the Allahabad High Court, assisted by Krishna Kant Malaviya, and secured acquittals or commutation for most of them, with the death sentences finally confined to nineteen. Neither C. R. Das, nor Kitchlew and Nizami, nor Jinnah appeared in the Chauri Chaura appeals.

items.value: The Poona Pact
items.reasoning: Gandhi's fast unto death in Yerawada jail against the separate electorates granted to the Depressed Classes by the Communal Award ended with the Poona Pact of September 1932. Immediately afterwards he made the removal of untouchability a formal plank of his programme: the All India Anti-Untouchability League (soon renamed the Harijan Sevak Sangh) was founded in September 1932, the weekly Harijan began in 1933, and he undertook a countrywide Harijan tour in 1933-34. The Delhi Pact of 1931, the 1942 arrests and the Government of India Act, 1935 have no such connection.

items.value: All three — papaya, pineapple and guava were brought to India by the Portuguese
items.reasoning: All three are New World fruits with no pre-Columbian presence in India. Papaya, native to Central America, and guava, native to Mexico and Central America, were carried into India by the Portuguese in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and pineapple, native to Brazil and Paraguay, was introduced by them around the middle of the sixteenth century. They belong with the same Portuguese introductions as cashew, sapota, custard apple, chilli, potato and tobacco.
